title: Satisfied and Satisfying
hookLine: a cook who eats last and fills every plate, and a goddess whose open hand pours coins
carry: lakshmi's fortune is meant to flow outward
tomorrow: why do some Hindus go to Lakshmi first?
last: MAY SHE BE PLEASED WITH ME.

cards: At a big family dinner there's often one person who eats last. She's been at the stove since noon. She notices your plate is empty before you do, and fills it, and fills the next one.
And when she finally sits down, she doesn't look tired so much as content, the way someone looks when they had enough to give. The Sri Sukta has a phrase for that.
Today the hymn stops calling the goddess and starts describing her, and one pair of words sits right in the middle.

teach.h: SHE ROSE FROM THE OCEAN OF MILK.
teach.b: First, where she comes from. The Puranas tell that when the gods and the demons churned the ocean of milk, treasures rose out of it one by one, and then Lakshmi rose, seated on a lotus, and the whole world brightened.
The Sri Sukta paints her in that light. Here's the line, in paraphrase.

Smiling, within a wall of gold, moist and blazing, satisfied and satisfying, standing on the lotus, the color of the lotus: I call Sri near. Start with the strange pairing: moist and blazing. Wet and on fire at once.
Some readers hear tenderness and radiance; others, the monsoon and the sun a field needs. The hymn lets her hold both.
Then the pair this day is about: satisfied, and satisfying. In Sanskrit the two words echo, triptam tarpayantim. She is full, and she makes others full.
Notice the order. Her fullness comes first, and the filling flows out of it. That's the cook at the dinner table: she isn't giving from an empty pot.
And here's the teaching families see every Diwali.
In so many pictures of Lakshmi, gold coins pour from her open hand. Her wealth isn't locked behind the gold wall; it spills.

Many Hindus take that as how fortune should move through a home: what comes in goes out again, as sweets carried to the neighbors, gifts, and giving to people in need. A goddess of wealth who hoards wouldn't be Lakshmi.
She's smiling, soft and bright. She has enough, and so she shares.

how: Images of Lakshmi in homes and temples often show her seated or standing on a lotus, and the Sri Sukta's descriptions of her are chanted in front of such images during Lakshmi worship.

o: a rule that only the rich may chant this hymn
a hymn for a feast held for the gods each year
a hymn picturing Sri as full, and filling others

p: water and fire in one portrait
she stands on it, and is its color

s: the hymn pictures Sri as stern and frowning
she's smiling, soft and bright, within a wall of gold.
she is called both satisfied and satisfying
triptam tarpayantim: full herself, and making others full.
in many pictures of Lakshmi, coins pour from her open hand
her fortune spills outward: satisfied, and satisfying.

games.q: it's Diwali, and a lot has come your way this year. the Sri Sukta's goddess is satisfied and satisfying. what does that ask of you?
o: lock it up so it stays.
let some of it flow out to others.
give it all away and keep nothing.
games.why: she's full, and so she fills. in pictures her coins pour outward, and many families give at Diwali for the same reason.

practice: Let the breath come in all the way, without forcing it, and go out slowly, as if you're giving it away: in until you're full, out as a gift.

If a face comes to mind, someone who could use a little of what you have, let them sit with you on the out-breath, and choose one small thing to share with them this week: a sweet, a call, a little money.
If you pray, you can offer them to the goddess, or to God; if you don't, just keep breathing in and giving out.

wordCard.voice: The Sri Sukta. A hymn that paints Sri smiling, moist and blazing, standing on the lotus: satisfied, and satisfying.

orig.note: Sanskrit: tṛptāṃ tarpayantīm, 'satisfied, and satisfying,' from the Sri Sukta's portrait of Sri.

carryVoice: Your line: Lakshmi's fortune is meant to flow outward. Full first, and then the filling flows. Until tomorrow.
